subject: physics
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} question that tests this idea: "{lo}". Then score my answer the way an AP reader would.
promptWeak: Explain this {board} idea simply, with a worked example and the most common mistake students make: "{lo}".

questions.q: A suitcase rests on a rack in a train moving at constant velocity. A passenger on the train says that the suitcase’s translational kinetic energy is zero. A person standing on the platform says that it is (1/2)mv², where m is the suitcase’s mass and v the train’s speed. Which claim, with its reasoning, is correct?
options: The platform observer alone is correct, since speeds must all be measured relative to the ground.
Neither can be right unless they agree, since energy is conserved and the same for every observer.
The passenger alone is correct, since the suitcase is at rest on the rack that supports it.
Both are correct, since K depends on the speed measured in each observer’s frame of reference.
optionWhy: A student who thinks the ground is the one true frame picks this. A frame moving at constant velocity relative to the ground is just as valid; the passenger’s value is correct in the train’s frame.
A student who thinks energy conservation forces all observers to agree picks this. Conservation applies within one frame; different frames measure different speeds and so different kinetic energies.

A student who takes motion relative to an object’s support as its true motion picks this. Relative to the platform the suitcase moves with the train, and the platform observer’s value is correct in that frame.

Kinetic energy is (1/2)mv² with v the speed in a chosen frame. The suitcase is at rest relative to the train and moves at the train’s speed relative to the platform, so both values are right, each in its own frame.
questions.explain: Kinetic energy is (1/2)mv² with v the speed in a chosen frame. The suitcase is at rest relative to the train and moves at the train’s speed relative to the platform, so both values are right, each in its own frame.

questions.q: A cart moves along a straight track at constant speed u relative to the ground. A small puck of mass m slides on the cart’s frictionless floor at speed v relative to the cart, in the same direction as the cart moves. By how much does the puck’s translational kinetic energy measured by an observer at rest on the ground exceed the value measured by an observer riding on the cart?
optionWhy: A student who adds kinetic energies from frame to frame picks this: K_ground = K_cart + (1/2)mu², so the difference is (1/2)mu². Velocities add between frames, but kinetic energy depends on the square of the total speed, (u + v)², which adds the cross term muv.
Relative to the ground the velocities add: the puck’s speed is u + v, since both motions are in the same direction. The difference is (1/2)m(u + v)² − (1/2)mv² = (1/2)mu² + muv = mu(u + 2v)/2.
A student who writes kinetic energy as mv², dropping the factor 1/2, picks this: m(u + v)² − mv² = mu² + 2muv. With K = (1/2)mv² in each frame, the difference is half of this.
A student who takes kinetic energy as proportional to speed picks this: (1/2)m(u + v) − (1/2)mv = (1/2)mu. Its units, kg·m/s, are not those of energy; the speeds must be squared before subtracting.
questions.explain: Relative to the ground the velocities add: the puck’s speed is u + v, since both motions are in the same direction. The difference is (1/2)m(u + v)² − (1/2)mv² = (1/2)mu² + muv = mu(u + 2v)/2.
questions.working: (1/2)m(u + v)² − (1/2)mv² = (1/2)mu² + muv = mu(u + 2v)/2 (sympy-checked). Distractors: K_ground = K_cart + (1/2)mu² gives mu²/2; m(u + v)² − mv² (no 1/2) gives mu(u + 2v); (1/2)m(u + v) − (1/2)mv (K ∝ speed) gives mu/2.

questions.q: The figure shows three objects, A, B and C, sliding along a straight horizontal line, with their masses and velocities labeled. K_A, K_B and K_C are their translational kinetic energies. Which ranking is correct?
optionWhy: K = (1/2)mv²: K_A = (1/2)(1.0)(3.0)² = 4.5 J, K_B = (1/2)(1.0)(5.0)² = 12.5 J, K_C = (1/2)(4.0)(2.0)² = 8.0 J. B’s direction does not matter, because K depends on speed only.
A student who takes kinetic energy as proportional to speed (mv) picks this: 3.0, 5.0 and 8.0 for A, B and C. The speed is squared in K, which favors the fast, light object B over the slow, heavy C.
A student who thinks mass does not affect kinetic energy picks this, ranking by speed alone. C’s mass is four times A’s, which more than makes up for its lower speed: 8.0 J against 4.5 J.
A student who gives B a negative kinetic energy because it moves to the left picks this. The velocity is squared in K = (1/2)mv², so K is positive whichever way an object moves.
questions.explain: K = (1/2)mv²: K_A = (1/2)(1.0)(3.0)² = 4.5 J, K_B = (1/2)(1.0)(5.0)² = 12.5 J, K_C = (1/2)(4.0)(2.0)² = 8.0 J. B’s direction does not matter, because K depends on speed only.
questions.working: K_A = 4.5 J, K_B = 12.5 J, K_C = 8.0 J ⇒ K_B > K_C > K_A. mv: 3.0, 5.0, 8.0 ⇒ C > B > A; speed: B > A > C; with B negative: C > A > B.

questions.q: A block of mass m slides onto a rough horizontal patch with speed v₀. On the patch, the coefficient of kinetic friction increases with the distance x the block has moved into the patch as μ_k = bx, where b is a positive constant. Air resistance is negligible, and g is the magnitude of the gravitational field. How far into the patch does the block slide before it stops?
optionWhy: The friction force is μ_k mg = bmgx, so its work over the slide is −∫₀ᴰ bmgx dx = −bmgD²/2. By the work–energy theorem this equals the change in kinetic energy, −(1/2)mv₀², so D² = v₀²/(bg) and D = v₀/√(bg).

A student who multiplies the friction force at the end of the slide, bmgD, by the whole distance D picks this: bmgD² = (1/2)mv₀². The force grows from zero, so its work is the integral of the force over the path, bmgD²/2, half as much.
A student who writes the block’s kinetic energy as mv₀², leaving out the ½, picks this: bmgD²/2 = mv₀² gives D = v₀√(2/(bg)). The block’s initial kinetic energy is (1/2)mv₀².
A student who takes kinetic energy to be proportional to speed rather than to its square picks this: bmgD²/2 = (1/2)mv₀ gives D = √(v₀/(bg)), which does not even have the units of length.
questions.explain: The friction force is μ_k mg = bmgx, so its work over the slide is −∫₀ᴰ bmgx dx = −bmgD²/2. By the work–energy theorem this equals the change in kinetic energy, −(1/2)mv₀², so D² = v₀²/(bg) and D = v₀/√(bg).
questions.working: F_N = mg on the level patch, so the friction force has magnitude μ_k mg = bmgx, opposite the motion. Work done by friction over the slide: W_f = ∫₀ᴰ (−bmgx) dx = −bmgD²/2. Work–energy theorem (friction is the only force with a component along the motion): W_f = ΔK = 0 − (1/2)mv₀², so bmgD²/2 = (1/2)mv₀² and D = v₀/√(bg) (sympy-checked; b in 1/m, so D is in m). Distractors: friction at the end of the slide times D, bmgD² = (1/2)mv₀², D = v₀/√(2bg); K written as mv₀², bmgD²/2 = mv₀², D = v₀√(2/(bg)); K taken as proportional to v₀, bmgD²/2 = (1/2)mv₀, D = √(v₀/(bg)).

questions.q: An object of mass m starts from rest at x = 0. The graph shows the only force with a component along its motion, F, as a function of position x. The object’s speed at x = 4x₀ can be written as v = k√(F₀x₀/m). What is the value of k?
optionWhy: A student who adds the area below the axis as positive work picks this: total 2.5F₀x₀, v = √5 √(F₀x₀/m). The force is opposite to the motion between 3x₀ and 4x₀, so that area is negative work.

A student who uses the largest force, F₀, as if it were exerted over the whole 4x₀ picks this: W = 4F₀x₀, v = √8 √(F₀x₀/m). The work is the area under the graph, not the peak force times the displacement.
A student who writes the kinetic energy as mv² picks this: mv² = 1.5F₀x₀, v = √1.5 √(F₀x₀/m). With K = (1/2)mv² the speed is √2 times larger.

The work is the signed area under the graph: (1/2)F₀x₀ from 0 to x₀, F₀x₀ from x₀ to 2x₀, +(1/2)F₀x₀ from 2x₀ to 3x₀ and −(1/2)F₀x₀ from 3x₀ to 4x₀, a total of (3/2)F₀x₀. (1/2)mv² = (3/2)F₀x₀ gives v = √3 √(F₀x₀/m) = 1.73√(F₀x₀/m).
questions.explain: The work is the signed area under the graph: (1/2)F₀x₀ from 0 to x₀, F₀x₀ from x₀ to 2x₀, +(1/2)F₀x₀ from 2x₀ to 3x₀ and −(1/2)F₀x₀ from 3x₀ to 4x₀, a total of (3/2)F₀x₀. (1/2)mv² = (3/2)F₀x₀ gives v = √3 √(F₀x₀/m) = 1.73√(F₀x₀/m).
questions.working: Areas: ½F₀x₀ + F₀x₀ + ½F₀x₀ − ½F₀x₀ = 1.5F₀x₀ = W_net = ½mv² ⇒ v = √(3F₀x₀/m) = 1.732√(F₀x₀/m) (sympy-checked). Distractors: magnitudes 2.5 → √5 = 2.24; F₀ × 4x₀ → √8 = 2.83; no ½ → √1.5 = 1.22.

questions.q: The graph shows the component F of the net force on an object along its direction of motion, as a function of the object’s position x. W₁, W₂ and W₃ are the work done by this force in the intervals marked 1, 2 and 3. Which ranking is correct?
optionWhy: A student who adds areas without signs picks this: 6 J, 1.5 J + 1.5 J = 3 J and 3 J. Area below the axis is negative work, so W₂ = 0 and W₃ = −3 J.
A student who ranks the intervals by the slope of the graph picks this: +1.5 N/m, 0 and −3 N/m. The slope tells how quickly the force changes, not the work it does.

The work in each interval is the signed area between the graph and the x-axis. Interval 1: (3 N)(2 m) = +6 J. Interval 2: the line falls from 3 N to −3 N, so equal triangles above and below the axis cancel: 0 J. Interval 3: the triangle from −3 N to 0 lies below the axis: −3 J. So W₁ > W₂ > W₃.

A student who ranks by the value of the force at the end of each interval picks this: 3 N, 0 and −3 N for intervals 1, 3 and 2. The work is the area under the graph over the interval, not its height at one point.
questions.explain: The work in each interval is the signed area between the graph and the x-axis. Interval 1: (3 N)(2 m) = +6 J. Interval 2: the line falls from 3 N to −3 N, so equal triangles above and below the axis cancel: 0 J. Interval 3: the triangle from −3 N to 0 lies below the axis: −3 J. So W₁ > W₂ > W₃.
questions.working: Signed areas: interval 1 (0–2 m): 3 × 2 = +6 J. Interval 2 (2–4 m): F from +3 to −3, zero at 3 m: +1.5 − 1.5 = 0 J. Interval 3 (4–6 m): F from −3 to 0: −½(2)(3) = −3 J. Distractors: magnitudes 6, 3, 3; slopes 0, −3, +1.5 N/m; end values 3, −3, 0 N.

questions.q: A skater stands at rest on frictionless ice facing a wall. She pushes on the wall with her hands, extending her arms, and glides away. The skater is the system. Which claim about the work done on her by the wall’s force, with its justification, is correct?
options: Positive: the wall’s force is what speeds her up, so it must transfer energy to her.
Positive: it equals the wall’s force multiplied by the time her hands push on the wall.
Zero: her hands, where the wall’s force is exerted, do not move while she pushes the wall.
Zero: the wall’s force on her and her force on the wall cancel, so no net force acts on her.
optionWhy: A student who thinks any force that speeds a system up must do work on it picks this. The wall’s force does accelerate her, but its point of application does not move, so it transfers no energy.
A student who thinks work depends on how long a force is exerted picks this. Work involves the displacement of the point of application, which is zero here; force times time is a different quantity.

Work is done by a force only if its point of application moves. Her hands stay against the wall during the push, so the wall’s force does no work, even though it is the external force that accelerates her. She cannot be modeled as an object, because her center of mass moves while the point of application does not; her kinetic energy comes from her own internal energy.

A student who thinks a third-law pair cancels picks this. The two forces are exerted on different objects; the wall’s force is unbalanced on her and accelerates her. The work is zero for a different reason: her hands do not move.
questions.explain: Work is done by a force only if its point of application moves. Her hands stay against the wall during the push, so the wall’s force does no work, even though it is the external force that accelerates her. She cannot be modeled as an object, because her center of mass moves while the point of application does not; her kinetic energy comes from her own internal energy.

questions.q: A narrow tunnel is drilled straight through the center of a uniform spherical planet of mass M and radius R. When an object of mass m is in the tunnel at a distance r from the planet’s center, the gravitational force exerted on it by the planet has magnitude GMmr/R³ and is directed toward the center, where G is the universal gravitational constant. With U_g = 0 when the object and the planet are infinitely far apart, what is the gravitational potential energy of the object–planet system when the object is at the planet’s center?
optionWhy: A student who takes ΔU as +∫F⃗ · dr⃗ picks this. That makes ΔU = +GMm/(2R) and U = −GMm/R + GMm/(2R). Gravity does positive work on the object as it moves toward the center, so U must decrease, not increase.

At the surface U_g = −GMm/R. Moving in to the center, ΔU = −∫_R^0 F_r dr with F_r = −GMmr/R³, which gives ΔU = −GMm/(2R): gravity does positive work as the object moves toward the center, so U decreases. U at the center is −GMm/R − GMm/(2R) = −3GMm/(2R).

A student who uses ΔU_g = mgΔy with the surface value g = GM/R² over the whole distance R picks this: ΔU = −GMm/R, so U = −2GMm/R. Inside the planet the field weakens steadily to zero at the center, so the true decrease is only half as large.

A student who thinks a conservative force does no work, so that U stays the same, picks this: the surface value −GMm/R. Gravity does positive work on the object as it moves from the surface to the center, so U decreases.
questions.explain: At the surface U_g = −GMm/R. Moving in to the center, ΔU = −∫_R^0 F_r dr with F_r = −GMmr/R³, which gives ΔU = −GMm/(2R): gravity does positive work as the object moves toward the center, so U decreases. U at the center is −GMm/R − GMm/(2R) = −3GMm/(2R).
questions.working: At the surface (r = R), outside-sphere form with U_g = 0 at infinity: U(R) = −GMm/R. Inside, the radial component of the force is F_r = −GMmr/R³ (toward the center). From the surface to the center: ΔU = −∫_R^0 F_r dr = −∫_R^0 (−GMmr/R³) dr = (GMm/R³)[r²/2]_R^0 = −GMm/(2R). U(0) = U(R) + ΔU = −GMm/R − GMm/(2R) = −3GMm/(2R). Distractors: ΔU = +∫F_r dr = +GMm/(2R) gives −GMm/(2R); mgΔy with surface g = GM/R² and Δy = −R gives ΔU = −GMm/R and U(0) = −2GMm/R; ΔU = 0 gives −GMm/R. Checked with sympy (G = 1.3, M = 2.1, m = 0.7, R = 1.9: −1.509, −0.503, −2.012, −1.006).

questions.q: The figure shows three identical small spheres, each of mass m, fixed in place, and the position (dashed circle) at which a fourth identical sphere is fixed after it is brought from very far away. Let U₀ = Gm²/s, where s is the distance labeled in the figure. With U_g = 0 for each pair at infinite separation, what is the change in the gravitational potential energy of the system of four spheres?
optionWhy: A student who counts only the fourth sphere’s nearest neighbors picks this, leaving out the sphere at the opposite corner. Every pair interacts gravitationally, so the diagonal pair adds −U₀/√2.

The total potential energy is the sum over pairs, and only the three pairs that include the fourth sphere change. Two of the other spheres are a distance s away and one is a distance √2 s away (the diagonal): ΔU = −Gm²/s − Gm²/s − Gm²/(√2 s) = −(2 + 1/√2)U₀ ≈ −2.7U₀.

A student who gives the total potential energy of the final four-sphere system, −(4 + √2)U₀, picks this. The question asks for the change; the three pairs among the spheres already in place are unchanged.

A student who adds the three pair energies as vectors pointing from the fourth sphere toward the others picks this: the two side pairs combine at right angles to √2 U₀ along the diagonal, plus U₀/√2 along the diagonal, giving −2.1U₀. Potential energies are scalars and add as numbers.
questions.explain: The total potential energy is the sum over pairs, and only the three pairs that include the fourth sphere change. Two of the other spheres are a distance s away and one is a distance √2 s away (the diagonal): ΔU = −Gm²/s − Gm²/s − Gm²/(√2 s) = −(2 + 1/√2)U₀ ≈ −2.7U₀.
questions.working: New pairs: two at distance s, one at √2 s. ΔU = −Gm²(2/s + 1/(√2 s)) = −(2 + 1/√2)U₀ = −2.71U₀. Distractors: nearest neighbors only → −2.0U₀; total of all six pairs, −(4 + √2)U₀ → −5.4U₀; vector sum, −(√2 + 1/√2)U₀ → −2.1U₀.

questions.q: An object of mass m is raised from Earth’s surface to a height h that is not small compared with Earth’s radius. ΔU_exact is the change in the gravitational potential energy of the object–Earth system calculated from U_g = −Gm_1m_2/r, and ΔU_approx = mgh, where g is the gravitational field strength at Earth’s surface. Which comparison is correct?
options: ΔU_exact = ΔU_approx, because mgΔy is exact for every height above Earth.
ΔU_exact > ΔU_approx, because the gravitational field grows stronger with height.
ΔU_exact < 0 < ΔU_approx, because U_g found from −Gm_1m_2/r is negative.
ΔU_exact < ΔU_approx, because the gravitational field weakens with height.
optionWhy: A student who thinks mgΔy holds at any height picks this. It treats the field as constant, which is accurate only for heights small compared with Earth’s radius; here the field weakens noticeably along the way.
A student who thinks gravity is stronger higher up picks this. The field strength GM/r² decreases as r increases, so the exact change is smaller than mgh.
A student who confuses the sign of U_g with the sign of its change picks this. U_g is negative at every height, but it increases toward zero as the object rises, so ΔU_exact is positive.

mgh assumes the field keeps its surface value all the way up. The field strength GM/r² decreases with distance from Earth’s center, so less energy is stored per meter at greater heights: ΔU_exact = mgh·R/(R + h), which is less than mgh.
questions.explain: mgh assumes the field keeps its surface value all the way up. The field strength GM/r² decreases with distance from Earth’s center, so less energy is stored per meter at greater heights: ΔU_exact = mgh·R/(R + h), which is less than mgh.
questions.working: ΔU_exact = GMm(1/R − 1/(R + h)) = GMmh/(R(R + h)) = mgh·R/(R + h) with g = GM/R². R/(R + h) < 1, so 0 < ΔU_exact < mgh.

questions.q: Two uniform spheres are far from all other objects. The distance between their centers is tripled. With U_g = 0 at infinite separation, how does the gravitational potential energy of the two-sphere system change?
options: Its magnitude becomes one-ninth as large, so U_g also increases.
Its magnitude becomes one-third as large, so U_g increases.
Its magnitude becomes one-third as large, and so U_g decreases.
Its magnitude becomes three times as large, so U_g decreases.
optionWhy: A student who uses a 1/r² dependence, as for the gravitational force, picks this. U_g is proportional to 1/r, so its magnitude becomes one-third as large.
U_g = −Gm_1m_2/r: tripling r makes the magnitude one-third as large. U_g is negative, so a smaller magnitude means a larger value: U_g increases toward zero as the spheres move apart.
A student who drops the minus sign, U_g = +Gm_1m_2/r, picks this. With the minus sign, a smaller magnitude means a less negative, larger U_g.

A student who takes the magnitude of U_g to grow in proportion to separation, as mgΔy grows with height, picks this; with the negative sign kept, a larger magnitude means a lower U_g. The magnitude is proportional to 1/r, so it becomes one-third as large.
questions.explain: U_g = −Gm_1m_2/r: tripling r makes the magnitude one-third as large. U_g is negative, so a smaller magnitude means a larger value: U_g increases toward zero as the spheres move apart.
questions.working: |U_g| ∝ 1/r → ×1/3; U_g < 0, so U_g increases (from −X to −X/3). Distractors: ∝ 1/r² → ×1/9; sign dropped → decreases; ∝ r → ×3 (more negative).

questions.q: A uniform flexible rope of mass M and length L lies straight on a frictionless horizontal table, perpendicular to the table’s edge, with one-quarter of its length hanging vertically over the smooth edge. The rope is released from rest and slides off the table. Air resistance is negligible, and g is the magnitude of the gravitational field. What is the speed of the rope at the instant its upper end leaves the table?
optionWhy: A student who writes the rope’s kinetic energy as Mv² picks this: Mv² = 15MgL/32, so v² = 15gL/32. Kinetic energy is (1/2)Mv², so the speed is larger by a factor of √2.
Using centers of mass, the rope–Earth system’s U_g falls from −(M/4)g(L/8) = −MgL/32 to −MgL/2, a decrease of 15MgL/32. This equals (1/2)Mv², so v² = 15gL/16 and v = 0.97√(gL).

A student who finds the work done by a varying force as its final value times the distance picks this: Mg(3L/4) = (1/2)Mv², so v² = 3gL/2. The pull of gravity on the hanging part grows from Mg/4 to Mg as the rope slides, so the work done is less than Mg(3L/4).

A student who keeps the starting acceleration g/4 for the whole motion picks this: v² = 2(g/4)(3L/4) = 3gL/8. The hanging part, and so the net force and the acceleration, grow as the rope slides, so the rope ends up faster than this.
questions.explain: Using centers of mass, the rope–Earth system’s U_g falls from −(M/4)g(L/8) = −MgL/32 to −MgL/2, a decrease of 15MgL/32. This equals (1/2)Mv², so v² = 15gL/16 and v = 0.97√(gL).
questions.working: System: rope and Earth; the table’s normal force does no work and there is no friction, so K + U_g is constant. Take U_g = 0 at the table top. Initially the hanging quarter (mass M/4) has its center of mass L/8 below the table: U_i = −(M/4)g(L/8) = −MgL/32. Finally the whole rope hangs with its center of mass L/2 below the table: U_f = −MgL/2. (1/2)Mv² = U_i − U_f = 15MgL/32, so v² = 15gL/16 and v = √(15/16)√(gL) = 0.97√(gL). Check by integration: W = ∫_0^(3L/4) (Mg(L/4 + s)/L) ds = 15MgL/32, the same. Distractors: K = Mv² gives v² = 15gL/32, v = 0.68√(gL); the final pull Mg times the distance 3L/4 gives v² = 3gL/2, v = 1.22√(gL); the starting acceleration g/4 kept over 3L/4 gives v² = 3gL/8, v = 0.61√(gL). Checked with sympy.

questions.q: A 2.0 kg block is released from rest and slides 5.0 m down a rough incline that makes an angle of 37° with the horizontal. The coefficient of kinetic friction between the block and the incline is 0.25. Air resistance is negligible. Use g = 10 m/s², sin 37° = 0.60 and cos 37° = 0.80. What is the block's speed after it has slid 5.0 m?
optionWhy: A student who thinks mechanical energy is always conserved picks this, converting all 60 J of U_g into K. Friction does −20 J of work on the block, so only 40 J becomes kinetic energy.
A student who takes the normal force to be mg = 20 N picks this: friction 5.0 N does −25 J, leaving K = 35 J. On the incline F_N = mg cos 37° = 16 N, so friction is 4.0 N.

The block–Earth system loses mg(5.0 × 0.60) = 60 J of U_g. Kinetic friction, 0.25 × mg cos 37° = 4.0 N, does −20 J of work on it over 5.0 m, transferring that energy out (it is dissipated as thermal energy and sound). So K = 40 J and v = √(2 × 40/2.0) ≈ 6.3 m/s.
A student who uses the 5.0 m slid along the incline as the drop in height picks this: ΔU_g = −100 J and K = 80 J. The drop is 5.0 m × sin 37° = 3.0 m.
questions.explain: The block–Earth system loses mg(5.0 × 0.60) = 60 J of U_g. Kinetic friction, 0.25 × mg cos 37° = 4.0 N, does −20 J of work on it over 5.0 m, transferring that energy out (it is dissipated as thermal energy and sound). So K = 40 J and v = √(2 × 40/2.0) ≈ 6.3 m/s.
questions.working: System: block and Earth; the incline is outside, and its friction does negative work. Drop: (5.0 m)(0.60) = 3.0 m, so ΔU_g = −(2.0)(10)(3.0) = −60 J. F_N = mg cos 37° = 16 N; F_f = 0.25 × 16 N = 4.0 N; W_f = −(4.0 N)(5.0 m) = −20 J. ΔK = 60 J − 20 J = 40 J = (1/2)(2.0 kg)v², v = √40 ≈ 6.3 m/s.

questions.q: A sled slides down a snowy hill. The graph shows the kinetic energy K and the gravitational potential energy U_g of the sled–Earth system as functions of the sled's horizontal position x. A student claims that energy was transferred between the sled–Earth system and its surroundings as the sled moved from x = 0 to x = 40 m. Which statement from the graph correctly supports the claim?
options: K rises by 4 kJ between x = 0 and 40 m, so energy was transferred into the system.
U_g falls by 6 kJ between x = 0 and 40 m, so the mechanical energy fell by 6 kJ.
U_g falls by 6 kJ, but K rises by only 4 kJ, so K + U_g is 2 kJ lower at 40 m.
U_g is 0 kJ at x = 40 m, which shows that the sled–Earth system has no energy left there.
optionWhy: A student who thinks a gain in kinetic energy shows energy coming in from outside, even though Earth is in the system, picks this. The rise in K comes from the fall in U_g inside the system, and the net transfer is out of the system, not into it: K + U_g falls by 2 kJ.

A student who equates mechanical energy with potential energy picks this. Mechanical energy also includes K, which rose by 4 kJ, so the fall is only 2 kJ; a fall in U_g alone could all have become kinetic energy.

If no energy crossed the boundary of the sled–Earth system and nothing inside it were nonconservative, K + U_g would be constant. It falls from 6 kJ to 4 kJ, so 2 kJ left the system: the snow and the air did negative work on the sled, and the energy became thermal energy and sound.
A student who reads zero potential energy as 'no energy' picks this. The zero of U_g is a chosen reference level, and the system still has 4 kJ of kinetic energy at x = 40 m.
questions.explain: If no energy crossed the boundary of the sled–Earth system and nothing inside it were nonconservative, K + U_g would be constant. It falls from 6 kJ to 4 kJ, so 2 kJ left the system: the snow and the air did negative work on the sled, and the energy became thermal energy and sound.
questions.working: From the graph: at x = 0, K + U_g = 0 + 6 kJ = 6 kJ; at x = 40 m, K + U_g = 4 kJ + 0 = 4 kJ. Mechanical energy fell by 2 kJ, so with no nonconservative interactions inside the sled–Earth system, 2 kJ was transferred out by the negative work of the snow and air.

questions.q: The diagram shows the path of a ball thrown from level ground; T is the highest point of the path. Air resistance is negligible. Let v⃗ be the ball's velocity. A student claims that the gravitational force F⃗_g on the ball delivers zero power to it at T. Which statement correctly supports the claim?
options: At T, the ball is momentarily at rest, so its speed v is zero there.
At T, F⃗_g has done no work on the ball since the launch, so its power is zero.
At T, the upward force from the throw just balances F⃗_g, so their powers cancel.
At T, the force F⃗_g is perpendicular to v⃗, so it has no component along v⃗.
optionWhy: A student who thinks a projectile stops at the top of its path picks this. The ball lands some distance from its launch point, so it has a horizontal velocity that stays constant; at T only the vertical component of v⃗ is zero.

A student who treats power as the same thing as work picks this, and the premise is also false: the ball has risen to T, so gravity has done negative work on it since launch. Power is the rate of doing work at an instant, P = Fv cos θ, which is zero at T because θ = 90°.

A student who thinks the ball carries a force from the throw picks this. After release no upward force acts on the ball; gravity is the only force, and its power is zero at T because it is perpendicular to the velocity.

The power delivered by a constant force is P = Fv cos θ. The path shows the ball still moving sideways at T, so v⃗ is horizontal there, while F⃗_g points straight down: θ = 90° and cos θ = 0. Gravity delivers zero power at that instant, although F_g and v are both nonzero.
questions.explain: The power delivered by a constant force is P = Fv cos θ. The path shows the ball still moving sideways at T, so v⃗ is horizontal there, while F⃗_g points straight down: θ = 90° and cos θ = 0. Gravity delivers zero power at that instant, although F_g and v are both nonzero.

questions.q: A 6.0 kg cart starts from rest on a level, frictionless track. The graph shows the power delivered to the cart by the net force as a function of time. What is the cart's speed at t = 4.0 s?
optionWhy: A student who uses the power at t = 4.0 s as the average over the whole 4.0 s picks this: 12 W × 4.0 s = 48 J. The power rises from zero, so its average is 6 W and the energy is 24 J.
A student who reads the power at t = 4.0 s, 12 W, as the energy delivered, 12 J, picks this. Power is a rate; the energy is the area under the graph, 24 J.

Since P = dW/dt, the work done by the net force is the area under the P(t) graph: (1/2)(4.0 s)(12 W) = 24 J. That equals the cart's gain in kinetic energy, so (1/2)(6.0)v² = 24 and v = √8.0 ≈ 2.8 m/s.
A student who treats kinetic energy as proportional to speed picks this: (1/2)(6.0)v = 24 J gives 8.0 m/s. With K = (1/2)mv², v = √8.0 ≈ 2.8 m/s.
questions.explain: Since P = dW/dt, the work done by the net force is the area under the P(t) graph: (1/2)(4.0 s)(12 W) = 24 J. That equals the cart's gain in kinetic energy, so (1/2)(6.0)v² = 24 and v = √8.0 ≈ 2.8 m/s.
questions.working: Energy delivered = ∫P dt = area under P(t) = (1/2)(4.0 s)(12 W) = 24 J = ΔK. (1/2)(6.0 kg)v² = 24 J, so v = √8.0 ≈ 2.8 m/s.

questions.q: A car of mass m starts from rest on a level road. Its engine delivers a constant power P to the car, and friction and air resistance are negligible. What is the car's speed at time t?
optionWhy: The engine's work is the only work done on the car, so dK/dt = P. With P constant and K = 0 at t = 0, K = Pt. Then (1/2)mv² = Pt gives v = √(2Pt/m).

A student who assumes a constant force and acceleration picks this: F = ma = mv/t, and P = Fv = mv²/t gives v = √(Pt/m). With constant power the force P/v falls as the car speeds up, so the acceleration is not constant; integrate dK/dt = P instead.
A student who treats kinetic energy as proportional to speed picks this: (1/2)mv = Pt. This does not even have units of speed; K = (1/2)mv² needs a square root.
A student who treats the power as if it were a constant force picks this: a = P/m and v = at = Pt/m. Power is not a force, and the expression does not have units of speed; the driving force is P/v.
questions.explain: The engine's work is the only work done on the car, so dK/dt = P. With P constant and K = 0 at t = 0, K = Pt. Then (1/2)mv² = Pt gives v = √(2Pt/m).
questions.working: P = dW/dt = dK/dt, constant, so K = Pt (K = 0 at t = 0). (1/2)mv² = Pt, so v = √(2Pt/m). The force P/v decreases as v increases, so the acceleration is not constant.

questions.q: A satellite moves in an elliptical orbit around a planet of mass M. At point P of the orbit, it is at distance r from the planet's center and has speed v. Later it passes point Q, at distance 2r from the planet's center. Neither P nor Q is the closest or the farthest point of the orbit. What is the satellite's speed at Q?
optionWhy: A student who takes kinetic energy to be proportional to speed, writing K = (1/2)mv, gets (1/2)mv − GMm/r = (1/2)mv_Q − GMm/(2r) and so v_Q = v − GM/r. That expression does not even have units of speed; kinetic energy is (1/2)mv², which gives v_Q² = v² − GM/r.

A student who takes the satellite's angular momentum to be mvr at every point, so that vr is constant, picks this: v_Q(2r) = vr. Angular momentum is mvr sin θ; at P and Q the velocity is not perpendicular to the line from the planet's center, so the speeds are not in the inverse ratio of the distances.
The system's mechanical energy is the same at P and Q: (1/2)mv² − GMm/r = (1/2)mv_Q² − GMm/(2r). Solving, v_Q² = v² − GM/r. The satellite moves away from the planet, so it slows down.

A student who uses the circular-orbit speed √(GM/r) at Q, with the distance 2r, picks this. That speed holds only for a circular orbit; in an elliptical orbit the speed at Q follows from the conservation of mechanical energy.
questions.explain: The system's mechanical energy is the same at P and Q: (1/2)mv² − GMm/r = (1/2)mv_Q² − GMm/(2r). Solving, v_Q² = v² − GM/r. The satellite moves away from the planet, so it slows down.
questions.working: Only gravity acts, so the mechanical energy of the satellite–planet system is constant: (1/2)mv² − GMm/r = (1/2)mv_Q² − GMm/(2r). So v_Q² = v² − 2GM/r + GM/r = v² − GM/r, and v_Q = √(v² − GM/r). The satellite's angular momentum is also constant, but mvr sin θ involves angles that are not given, so it cannot give v_Q here. Distractors: K taken as (1/2)mv: v_Q = v − GM/r; vr taken as constant: v(r) = v_Q(2r), v_Q = v/2; circular-orbit speed at 2r: √(GM/(2r)).

questions.q: A satellite moves in an elliptical orbit around a planet of mass M. The satellite's closest and farthest distances from the planet's center are r_p and r_a. Which expression gives the satellite's speed at its closest point?
optionWhy: Conservation of angular momentum gives v_p r_p = v_a r_a, and conservation of energy gives (1/2)v_p² − GM/r_p = (1/2)v_a² − GM/r_a. Eliminating v_a: v_p² = 2GMr_a/(r_p(r_p + r_a)). The factor r_a/r_p > 1 makes v_p greater than v_a, as it must be.

A student who expects the satellite to move faster at the farther point assigns the smaller of the two speeds to the closest point. This expression is v_a; since v_p r_p = v_a r_a with r_p < r_a, the speed at the closest point is the larger one.

A student who uses energy conservation but takes the speed at the farthest point to be the circular-orbit speed √(GM/r_a) gets this. The satellite is not in a circular orbit at r_a; its speed there is fixed by angular momentum, v_a = v_p r_p/r_a.

A student who treats the gravitational field as constant at its value at the closest point, GM/r_p², and uses (1/2)v_p² − (1/2)v_a² = (GM/r_p²)(r_a − r_p) with v_a = v_p r_p/r_a, gets this. Over a change of distance comparable to r_p the field changes greatly, so U_g = −GMm/r must be used.
questions.explain: Conservation of angular momentum gives v_p r_p = v_a r_a, and conservation of energy gives (1/2)v_p² − GM/r_p = (1/2)v_a² − GM/r_a. Eliminating v_a: v_p² = 2GMr_a/(r_p(r_p + r_a)). The factor r_a/r_p > 1 makes v_p greater than v_a, as it must be.
questions.working: Angular momentum (velocity ⟂ radius at both points): v_p r_p = v_a r_a, so v_a = v_p r_p/r_a. Energy: (1/2)v_p² − GM/r_p = (1/2)v_a² − GM/r_a. Substituting: (1/2)v_p²(1 − r_p²/r_a²) = GM(1/r_p − 1/r_a) = GM(r_a − r_p)/(r_p r_a). With 1 − r_p²/r_a² = (r_a − r_p)(r_a + r_p)/r_a²: v_p² = 2GM r_a/(r_p(r_p + r_a)). (Checked with sympy.)

questions.q: A probe is launched straight up from the surface of a planet that has no atmosphere, with exactly the escape speed. The only force on it is the planet's gravity. Taking upward as positive, which graph shows the probe's velocity v as a function of time t after launch?
optionWhy: A student who thinks the planet's gravity stops acting beyond some distance picks the graph in which v levels off at a positive value. Gravity acts at every distance, so the probe keeps slowing, though ever more gently.

With zero mechanical energy, v = √(2GM/r) at every distance: always positive, decreasing as r increases. The decrease gets slower and slower because gravity weakens as 1/r², and v approaches zero only as the probe gets infinitely far away.

A student who thinks a probe whose velocity reaches zero stays at rest picks the graph that drops to zero and stays there. Zero velocity does not mean zero acceleration; besides, at escape speed v = √(2GM/r) is never zero at a finite distance.

A student who treats gravity as constant at its surface value picks the straight line: constant deceleration would stop the probe and bring it back. Gravity weakens with distance, so a probe at escape speed never stops at a finite distance.
questions.explain: With zero mechanical energy, v = √(2GM/r) at every distance: always positive, decreasing as r increases. The decrease gets slower and slower because gravity weakens as 1/r², and v approaches zero only as the probe gets infinitely far away.
questions.working: With E = 0, (1/2)mv² = GMm/r, so v = √(2GM/r) > 0 at every finite r: the probe never stops or turns back. Gravity, GMm/r², weakens as r grows, so v decreases ever more slowly, approaching zero only as r → ∞.

figure.alt: Four graphs, numbered 1 to 4, of velocity v (vertical axis, t axis across the middle) against time t, each starting at the same positive v. Panel 1: v decreases until partway along, then stays constant at a positive value. Panel 2: v decreases ever more slowly and is still above the t axis, and still decreasing, at the right edge. Panel 3: v falls to zero partway along and then stays at zero. Panel 4: a straight line falling steadily through zero halfway along to negative values.
